sources.title: Prevention and management of sternal wound infections

indications: Access for most cardiac operations: coronary bypass, valve and aortic surgery, and cardiac trauma.
Access to the anterior mediastinum: thymectomy, anterior mediastinal tumours, retrosternal goitre extension.
Bilateral lung or anterior lung access where a clamshell or bilateral thoracotomy is not chosen.
Emergency re-sternotomy after cardiac surgery for tamponade, bleeding or cardiac arrest not responding to initial measures.
contraindications: Active sternal or mediastinal infection, unless the purpose is debridement.
A re-operative chest with structures adherent to the sternum, where the approach must be modified (oscillating saw, peripheral cannulation first, CT planning) rather than abandoned.
Severe sternal deformity or previous radiotherapy, which change the approach and the closure.
Lesions better reached through a thoracotomy or minimally invasive approach.
preparation: Review the CT in any redo case: distance between the sternum and the right ventricle, aorta and patent grafts.
Infection prevention bundle per unit: screening and decolonisation for Staphylococcus aureus where used, glycaemic control, clipping rather than shaving, and timely prophylaxis.
For a redo or high-risk case, expose and prepare the groin or axillary vessels for peripheral cannulation before re-entry.
Emergency re-sternotomy set checked and stored at every cardiac surgical bedside.

Consent risks to discuss: bleeding and re-operation; sternal wound infection and mediastinitis; sternal instability and dehiscence; chronic chest wall pain; wire-related discomfort; injury to the heart or grafts during re-entry; brachial plexus injury from retraction.
positioning: Supine with the arms tucked at the sides and padded, or abducted per unit practice, with a small roll between the scapulae to lift the sternum.
Defibrillator pads applied before draping in redo and high-risk cases.
equipment: Sternal saw and an oscillating saw for re-entry; sternal retractor.
Stainless steel sternal wires and wire twisters; plates if reinforcement is planned.
Emergency re-sternotomy set: scalpel, wire cutters, retractor, suction, sterile gowns and gloves, internal defibrillator paddles.
anatomy: The sternum consists of the manubrium, body and xiphoid; the sternal angle marks the second costal cartilage.
The innominate (left brachiocephalic) vein crosses behind the manubrium, sometimes high in the neck, sometimes low.
The internal mammary arteries run vertically about one to two centimetres lateral to the sternal edge, behind the costal cartilages.
The right ventricle and, in a redo, adherent grafts lie immediately behind the lower sternum; the pleurae may reach the midline.
criticalSafety: Stop ventilation during the saw pass.
In a redo, never use the standard sternal saw for re-entry, and have peripheral cannulation sites prepared.
Counts must be correct before the sternum is closed: the mediastinum is a cavity.
Sternal wires close to the edge cut out; wires too lateral injure the mammary vessels.
After cardiac surgery, if early measures for arrest fail, reopen the chest within about five minutes (STS 2017).
structuresAtRisk: Patent bypass grafts in a redo
commonErrors: Opening the retractor too wide and too high.
Closing a high-risk sternum with standard wiring without considering reinforcement.
Delayed decision to reopen a bleeding or tamponading patient.
complications: Bleeding from the sternal edges, wire sites or mammary bed; tamponade.
Sternal wound infection, from superficial infection to deep sternal wound infection and mediastinitis.
Rib fracture and brachial plexus injury.
Injury to the heart or grafts at re-entry.
postop: Drain output monitoring with clear thresholds for calling the surgeon; correct coagulopathy and temperature.
Sternal precautions per unit, avoiding heavy lifting and pushing up with the arms in the early weeks.
Wound review for discharge, erythema, a clicking or unstable sternum, which suggest infection or dehiscence.
Re-sternotomy set and trained staff available at the bedside while the patient is in intensive care.

steps.emphasis: Include sternal infection, dehiscence and, in a redo, injury at re-entry.
State whether this is a redo, what lies behind the sternum on CT, and the plan for peripheral cannulation.
Timed prophylaxis per cardiac unit protocol with redosing for long cases and bypass; glycaemic control is part of sternal infection prevention.
Arms tucked and padded or supported, roll between the scapulae; external defibrillator pads before draping in a redo.
Chin to knees and both legs or arms if conduit may be needed; groins prepared for cannulation.
At the end of the cardiac procedure, after separation from bypass and decannulation.
Check the sternal edges, periosteum, mammary bed, thymic remnant, cannulation sites and pericardial edges in order.
Before the sternum is closed: the mediastinum and any opened pleura are cavities.
Close presternal fascia and subcutaneous tissue in layers over the wires, then skin; a sealed dressing.
Record the closure method and wire count, drains and pacing wires, and any concern about bleeding or sternal quality.
Taught here because it is part of every sternotomy's after-care: the whole team must know where the set is and who opens.

step.st.landmarks.title: Marking the midline
step.st.landmarks.why: Skin landmarks are misleading in obese patients and those with asymmetric chests. The midline of the bone, not the skin, determines a symmetric sternotomy.
how: Palpate the sternal notch and the xiphoid, and the intercostal spaces on both sides along the body of the sternum.
Mark the midline of the bone and keep the skin incision short of the notch where possible, for cosmesis and to reduce wound problems.
Divide subcutaneous tissue down to the periosteum in the same plane, without undermining.
structuresAtRisk: Presternal skin and subcutaneous blood supply
pitfalls: Following the skin midline when the sternum is rotated or the breasts pull the skin sideways.
Undermining presternal tissue, creating a dead space.

step.st.redo-entry.title: Re-entry in a previously opened chest
step.st.redo-entry.why: In a redo the right ventricle, aorta and patent grafts may be stuck to the back of the sternum, and injury at re-entry is a major cause of death in re-operative cardiac surgery.
how: Review the CT for structures adherent to the sternum before starting; prepare or cannulate peripheral vessels first when the risk is high.
Remove the old wires (or cut them and leave them in place as a guard until the saw has passed), and divide the anterior table with an oscillating saw.
Lift each half of the sternum with rakes and divide the posterior table and adhesions under direct vision, staying on the back of the bone.
If a structure is entered, control it with pressure and call for senior help; institute peripheral bypass before attempting repair if bleeding is major.
structuresAtRisk: Patent left internal mammary artery graft
pitfalls: Using the standard sternal saw for re-entry.
Dissecting the heart free before both sternal halves are lifted off it.

step.st.open-chest.title: Delayed sternal closure when the chest will not close safely
step.st.open-chest.why: Closing the sternum over a swollen heart or ongoing coagulopathic bleeding can cause tamponade physiology and haemodynamic collapse. Leaving the chest open is a deliberate, safe choice.
how: Consider leaving the sternum open when approximation causes hypotension, rising filling pressures or arrhythmia, or when diffuse bleeding needs packing.
Cover the open sternum with a sealed membrane or dressing per unit protocol, with drains in place, and keep the patient sedated and ventilated.
Plan return to theatre for wash-out and closure once the heart and coagulation have recovered, usually within days.
Record the reason, any packs left and their number in the operative note and handover.
structuresAtRisk: Heart and grafts beneath an open sternum
pitfalls: Forcing closure because an open chest feels like failure.
